reconcile.connective: JFB reads the Jerusalem decree as a matter of expediency — meant to avoid offending weaker brethren — rather than a claim that idol-meat is inherently wrong, so it still agrees with Paul's own "indifferent in themselves."

discrepancy.connective: Critical historian Gerd Lüdemann presses harder: Luke's Apostolic Decree is a later literary construction, and Paul's own letters, silent on any such decree even while addressing idol meat directly, show no awareness of it.

skeptic.name: Gerd Lüdemann
skeptic.work: The Acts of the Apostles: What Really Happened in the Earliest Days of the Church
skeptic.attribution: Gerd Lüdemann, The Acts of the Apostles: What Really Happened in the Earliest Days of the Church (Amherst, NY: Prometheus, 2005)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It was on the ground of Christian expediency, not to cause a stumbling-block to "weak" brethren, that the Jerusalem decree against partaking of such meats (though indifferent in themselves) was passed (Acts 15:1-29). Hence he here vindicates it against the Corinthian asserters of an inexpedient liberty.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reconciles Acts 15's decree with Paul's 'indifferent' teaching in 1 Cor 8 by reading the decree as a pastoral concession against giving offense, not a doctrinal claim that idol meat is intrinsically wrong.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871), on 1 Corinthians 8:7
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats this exact pairing directly at 1 Cor 8:7, reading the Acts 15 decree as an expediency measure rather than a claim that idol-meat is intrinsically defiling — harmonizing it with Paul's 'indifferent in themselves.' (Haley's Alleged Discrepancies has no section keyed to this Acts 15/1 Cor 8 pairing; its only 'Idol-meats' heading, p. 249, treats the internal 1 Cor 8/10 tension instead.)
